questions.scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration: your pipeline runs Claude Code on every pull request to post review comments. One instruction in the review prompt reads: "Make sure the code comments are correct." Over the last month developers have marked most comment-related findings as "not useful", and several have started collapsing the bot's review thread without reading it.
questions.stem: The team wants the comment-related findings to become trustworthy again with minimal changes to the rest of the pipeline. Which change is MOST effective?

options.text: Append a line telling the reviewer to post a comment issue only when it is highly confident the comment is wrong, so borderline cases are filtered out before posting.
Replace the instruction with a rule to flag a comment only when the behavior it describes contradicts what the code actually does, skipping wording or style nits.
Add a second Claude call that re-reads each comment finding and asks the model to confirm it against the same criteria before it is posted to the pull request.
Switch the review job to a larger model so it can better distinguish genuinely misleading comments from ones that are merely imprecise, terse or out of date.

questions.explanation: "Make sure the comments are correct" gives the model no decision rule, so it reports every phrasing it would have written differently. A **specific, categorical criterion** (described behavior contradicts actual behavior) defines exactly what counts as a finding and what to skip. That fixes the root cause of the false positives without adding calls or changing models. Anthropic's prompting guidance stresses being clear, direct and specific about what you want; vague goals produce inconsistent interpretation.

whyWrong.A: Confidence-based filtering does not define what a reportable issue is. The model can be highly confident that a terse comment is 'incorrect' under its own loose reading, so false positives persist.
whyWrong.C: Anthropic does recommend asking Claude to self-check, but a self-check is only as good as the criteria it checks against. This pass re-applies the same vague standard (correct), so it adds latency and cost without defining what to flag.
whyWrong.D: A bigger model still has to guess what 'accurate' means here. Model size does not supply missing criteria.

questions.mindset: When precision is poor, define what counts as a finding before adding filters, passes or bigger models.

questions.scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration: the automated PR reviewer reports findings in four categories: security, correctness bugs, performance and naming conventions. Dashboards show developers dismiss about 70% of naming findings but under 10% of security and correctness findings. In interviews, developers say they have started skimming past the whole review, including security warnings, because 'most of it is noise'.
questions.stem: Which action will MOST quickly restore developer trust in the review while the team works on improving quality?

options.text: Add "Be conservative and avoid nitpicking" to the system prompt so that all four categories produce fewer low-value findings in every review run.
Have the model attach a numeric confidence score to every finding in all four categories and suppress any finding that scores below a fixed threshold.
Add an evaluator agent that reviews every finding from the reviewer and votes on whether it deserves to be posted before anything appears.
Temporarily switch off the naming category, keep the working security and bug findings running, and refine the naming criteria before re-enabling it.

questions.explanation: A high false-positive category **erodes trust in the accurate categories** too, which is exactly what the interviews show. The fastest fix is to turn off the noisy category while you rewrite its criteria, leaving the high-precision categories (security, bugs) running so developers see that every posted finding matters. This is targeted, reversible and needs no new infrastructure.

whyWrong.A: 'Be conservative' is a vague directive that does not reliably change precision. It may also suppress real security findings, the category that is already working.
whyWrong.B: Self-reported confidence is not a reliable filter, and a global threshold treats the healthy categories the same as the broken one. Confidence-based filtering is what explicit criteria are meant to replace.
whyWrong.C: An extra voting agent is over-engineered for a problem isolated to one category. It adds cost and latency and still lacks a clear definition of a valid naming issue.

questions.mindset: Protect trust in the precise categories first. Switch off the noisy one, fix it, then bring it back.

questions.stem: A team's code-review prompt currently says: "Review this diff and report any problems you find." Reviewers complain about many low-value findings and inconsistent severity labels. Which TWO prompt changes will MOST improve precision and consistency? Choose TWO.

options.text: List what to report (bugs that change runtime behavior, security flaws) and what to skip (formatting, style preferences, patterns already used in the file).
Add the line "Only report problems you are at least 90% confident about" at the end of the prompt so low-certainty findings are excluded from the review.
Add a role line telling the model it is a principal engineer with twenty years of experience who holds very high standards for code quality on each review.
Define each severity level with explicit criteria and a short concrete code example showing a typical real issue that belongs at that level.
Add the instruction "Be careful and conservative; avoid nitpicking" near the top of the prompt so the model raises its bar before posting findings.

questions.explanation: Precision improves when the prompt states **categorical criteria**: what is in scope and what is explicitly out of scope (A). Severity becomes consistent when each level is **defined with concrete examples** (D), because the model can compare a new issue against a known anchor instead of guessing. Both changes give the model a decision rule rather than an attitude.

whyWrong.B: A numeric self-confidence threshold is not calibrated and does not define what a problem is. It is confidence-based filtering, which does not reliably raise precision.
whyWrong.C: A role can set tone and focus, but 'very high standards' may increase nitpicking. It does not say which issues to report or how to rate them.
whyWrong.E: 'Careful' and 'conservative' are vague directives. They do not tell the model which categories to drop, so behavior changes little or unpredictably.

questions.mindset: Replace adjectives (careful, conservative, confident) with categories and anchored examples.

questions.stem: A tech lead added "Report only findings you are highly confident in" to a review prompt, but the false-positive rate barely changed. She asks you for the most accurate explanation before trying anything else. What should you tell her?

options.text: The model's self-reported confidence is not a reliable filter, and the prompt never says which issue types count, so it needs explicit report and skip criteria.
The instruction was placed in the system prompt, where it carries less weight than user-turn content, so it should be moved into the user message to take effect.
The model needs a numeric confidence field added to the output schema, with a code filter that drops every finding scoring below 0.9 before it is posted.
Sampling temperature was left at its default, which makes the model's confidence judgments noisy, so setting temperature to zero will make the instruction work.

questions.explanation: Confidence-based phrasing asks the model to filter on a signal that is not well calibrated, and it leaves the real gap open: **no definition of what is worth reporting**. Explicit categorical criteria (report bugs and security issues; skip style and local conventions) are what move precision.

whyWrong.B: System prompts are an appropriate place for review rules. Moving a vague instruction to another turn does not make it specific.
whyWrong.C: This builds the same unreliable self-reported confidence into code. A threshold on an uncalibrated score is still confidence-based filtering, not a criterion.
whyWrong.D: Lower temperature can make outputs more repeatable, but it does not tell the model which findings are in scope. Consistent false positives are still false positives.

questions.mindset: Self-reported confidence is not a precision control. Criteria are.

questions.scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration: the PR reviewer labels each finding as critical, major or minor, and critical findings block the merge. Last week the same unchecked null dereference on a request handler was labeled critical in one PR and minor in another. The prompt currently says: "Assign a severity of critical, major or minor based on impact."
questions.stem: What is the BEST way to make severity labels consistent across pull requests?

options.text: Ask the model to write out its full reasoning about the likely production impact of each finding before it chooses a severity label for that finding.
Run the review three times in parallel for each pull request and assign each finding the severity label chosen by the majority of the three runs.
Give each severity level a written test (critical = can crash the app or expose data in production) plus one short code example of an issue at that level.
Remove the severity levels entirely and post every finding at a single level, leaving developers to decide which findings should block the merge.

questions.explanation: "Based on impact" leaves each run to invent its own scale. **Explicit severity criteria anchored by concrete code examples** give the model a fixed reference to classify against, so the same pattern lands at the same level. This is the direct, low-cost fix for inconsistent classification.

whyWrong.A: Reasoning first can help, but it reasons against an undefined scale, so two runs can still reach different conclusions about what 'critical' means.
whyWrong.B: Majority voting triples the cost and only averages over an undefined standard. It is over-engineered when the missing piece is the definition.
whyWrong.D: This removes useful information and the merge-blocking signal instead of fixing the classification.

questions.mindset: Consistency comes from anchored definitions, not from more runs.

questions.scenario: Multi-Agent Research System: a synthesis subagent merges findings from the search and document-analysis subagents and is told to "flag any contradictions between sources." Editors report that most flagged 'contradictions' are not real conflicts. For example, one study measured adoption in 2021 and another in 2024, or one surveyed only small businesses and another surveyed all firms.
questions.stem: Which change to the synthesis subagent's prompt will MOST effectively reduce these false contradiction flags?

options.text: Tell the synthesis subagent to be more careful, and to flag a contradiction only when it is genuinely certain the two sources really disagree with each other.
Define a contradiction as incompatible values for the same metric, population and time period, and record scope differences as context, not as conflicts.
Require every claim to be confirmed by at least two independent sources before the synthesis subagent includes it anywhere in the report.
Have the coordinator re-run the synthesis subagent whenever it flags a contradiction, and keep only the flags that appear in both of the two runs.

questions.explanation: The flags are false because the model has no definition of 'contradiction', so any difference looks like one. An **explicit categorical criterion** (same metric, same population, same period, incompatible values) separates true conflicts from differences in scope, and telling it where to record scope differences keeps that information instead of discarding it.

whyWrong.A: 'Be more careful' and 'genuinely certain' are vague confidence directives. They do not say what a contradiction is.
whyWrong.C: This changes the inclusion policy, not the contradiction definition. It would drop valid single-source findings and still mislabel scope differences.
whyWrong.D: Two runs that share the same undefined criterion tend to repeat the same false flags. It doubles the cost without fixing the cause.

questions.mindset: If the model keeps flagging the wrong thing, write down exactly what the thing is.

questions.scenario: Structured Data Extraction: a pipeline extracts key terms from vendor contracts and sets a flag_for_legal field when a clause is "anomalous". The legal team reviews every flagged contract and reports that about 80% of flags are standard boilerplate, such as ordinary limitation-of-liability language or routine confidentiality terms.
questions.stem: The legal team's review capacity is fixed. Which TWO changes will MOST effectively cut false flags while still catching real problems? Choose TWO.

options.text: Have the model output a confidence score with each flag and automatically discard any flag it scores below 0.8 confidence before human review.
Replace 'anomalous' with an enumerated list of clause conditions that must always be flagged and standard clause types that should never be flagged.
Change the instruction to 'only flag clauses that are truly unusual or concerning' so the model applies a stricter standard than it did before.
Route the contracts through a larger model in an overnight batch so that each contract receives more thorough analysis at a lower cost per document.
Add a few examples contrasting acceptable boilerplate with a genuinely problematic clause, briefly explaining why each one was or was not flagged.

questions.explanation: 'Anomalous' is undefined, so the model flags anything that looks legalistic. An **enumerated report/skip list** gives a categorical rule (B), and **contrasting examples** of acceptable versus problematic clauses (E) teach the boundary and help the model generalize to clause wordings the list did not name. Together they target false positives without hiding real issues.

whyWrong.A: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, so a fixed threshold can discard real issues while keeping confident false flags.
whyWrong.C: 'Truly unusual or concerning' is still vague. It shifts the bar by an unknown amount instead of defining it.
whyWrong.D: Batch processing changes cost and latency, not the criterion. A larger model still has to guess what 'anomalous' means.

questions.mindset: Precision comes from defining the boundary in words and showing it with examples.

questions.stem: A CI job asks Claude to point out missing tests in each pull request. Developers say it flags too many gaps that do not matter. Which rewritten instruction is MOST likely to reduce these false positives?

options.text: "Be thorough when looking for test gaps, but avoid flagging gaps that seem trivial or unimportant for the code's overall quality and maintainability."
"Only flag a test gap when you are confident it really matters for this codebase, and stay silent on any gap you are unsure about in this pull request."
"Review the tests the way an experienced QA lead on this team would, and report only the coverage gaps that such a reviewer would raise in review."
"Flag a gap only when a changed public function has a branch or error path that no test exercises; skip private helpers and generated code."

questions.explanation: Only option D gives a **testable, categorical rule**: which code is in scope (changed public functions), which condition triggers a finding (an unexercised branch or error path), and what to skip (private helpers, generated code). The other options rely on undefined judgments such as 'trivial', 'confident' or 'experienced'.

whyWrong.A: 'Trivial' and 'unimportant' are undefined, so each run draws the line differently.
whyWrong.B: This is confidence-based filtering. It does not say what makes a gap matter.
whyWrong.C: A persona does not specify criteria. The model must still guess what that reviewer would flag.

questions.mindset: A good criterion can be checked by someone who has never seen the prompt before.

questions.scenario: Structured Data Extraction: invoices are extracted with a tool whose JSON schema includes line_items and total. Your application validator checks that line-item amounts sum to the total. For one invoice the check fails: the line items sum to 1,240.00 but the extracted total is 1,420.00. The source PDF clearly shows a total of 1,240.00.
questions.stem: What is the MOST effective next request to send so the model can correct the extraction?

options.text: Resend the identical extraction request with temperature set to zero, so the model gives a more deterministic answer on its second attempt.
Resend the original request with an added line asking the model to be especially careful with all numbers and totals on this second attempt.
Send a follow-up with the original document, the failed extraction and the specific error: line items sum to 1,240.00 but the total says 1,420.00.
Send only the validation error message in a fresh request and ask the model to return just the corrected total as a single numeric field value.

questions.explanation: **Retry with error feedback** works best when the model sees everything it needs to self-correct: the source document, its previous output and the **specific** validation failure. Here the information is present in the source, so a targeted retry is likely to succeed.

whyWrong.A: A blind resend gives the model no signal about what went wrong. Temperature does not point it to the faulty field.
whyWrong.B: 'Be especially careful' is generic. It does not name the field or the discrepancy, so the same error can recur.
whyWrong.D: Without the document the model cannot check which value is right. It would have to guess.

questions.mindset: A useful retry includes the source, the failed output and the exact error.

questions.scenario: Structured Data Extraction: shipping notices are extracted into a schema where purchase_order_number is a required string. For a subset of notices, validation keeps failing because the extracted value is a placeholder or has an invalid format. Inspection shows those notices only say "PO: see attached", and the attachment is never sent to the pipeline.
questions.stem: The retry loop currently retries up to three times with error feedback. What should the architect do for these documents?

options.text: Make the field nullable, let the model return null for it, and route those notices to a human reviewer or an attachment-fetch step instead of retrying.
Increase the retry limit from three attempts to six and add more detailed wording about the expected purchase order number format to the field description.
Add few-shot examples showing correctly formatted purchase order numbers so that the model learns the expected pattern for this specific field.
Switch these notices to a larger, more capable model that is better at locating hard-to-find values within long or messy scanned documents.

questions.explanation: Retries fix **format and structural** errors. They cannot recover information that is **absent from the source**. A required field with no supporting data pressures the model to fabricate a value. Making it **nullable** and routing the case to a human or a step that fetches the attachment fixes the real gap.

whyWrong.B: More attempts cannot produce data that is not in the input. They waste tokens and raise the risk of a fabricated value passing validation.
whyWrong.C: Examples of the format make a fabricated-but-valid-looking number more likely, which is worse than a failure.
whyWrong.D: No model can extract a value that is not in the document it was given.

questions.mindset: Before retrying, ask whether the answer is actually in the input.

questions.scenario: Structured Data Extraction: a lease-abstraction pipeline validates each extraction and can retry once with the specific validation errors appended. The team wants to know which failures are worth retrying and which should go straight to human review.
questions.stem: Which TWO validation failures are MOST likely to be resolved by a retry with error feedback? Choose TWO.

options.text: The renewal option terms are defined only in a master agreement that the lease refers to, and that master agreement was not included in the input.
The commencement date was returned as "April 3, 2025" even though the schema description requires an ISO 8601 date such as 2025-04-03.
The tenant's signature date is missing because the signature page in the scanned lease document is blank and contains no visible date at all.
The security deposit amount was placed in the monthly_rent field and the rent amount in the deposit field, even though both are clearly labeled.
The landlord's tax ID is stored only in an external vendor database and is never written anywhere in the lease document that was provided.

questions.explanation: Retries with error feedback succeed when the correct information **is in the source** and the problem is how it was expressed or placed: a **format mismatch** (B) or **values in the wrong fields** (D). When the information exists only outside the provided input (A, E) or is not in the document at all (C), a retry cannot help and risks fabrication. Those cases need null handling and escalation.

whyWrong.A: The terms live in a document that was not provided. No amount of retrying puts them in the input.
whyWrong.C: The data is absent from the source. The right result is null plus human review, not a retry.
whyWrong.E: The value exists only in an external system. Fetch it from that system or route the case to review; do not ask the model to produce it.

questions.mindset: Retry fixes how the model expressed the data. It cannot create data that is missing from the input.

questions.stem: An expense-report extractor sometimes processes reports where the employee's handwritten total does not match the receipts listed. Finance wants these discrepancies caught, not hidden. What is the BEST design for the extraction output?

options.text: Instruct the model to correct the stated total so it matches the sum of the receipts, keeping the downstream expense data internally consistent.
Extract stated_total and a calculated_total from the receipts, plus a conflict_detected boolean, and route any mismatch to finance for review.
Instruct the model to return the total only when it matches the receipts, and to leave the field empty whenever the two values disagree.
Mark total as a required number field in a strict JSON schema so the model can never return an extraction without a valid numeric total.

questions.explanation: A **self-correction validation flow** captures both what the document says (stated_total) and what the parts add up to (calculated_total), and makes the inconsistency explicit with a **conflict_detected** flag. Application code can then check the values and route conflicts to humans. The source discrepancy is kept instead of being overwritten.

whyWrong.A: Silently 'fixing' the source hides exactly the discrepancy finance needs to see. The record no longer reflects the document.
whyWrong.C: Dropping the value loses information and gives no signal about why it is missing.
whyWrong.D: A schema guarantees a well-formed number, not a correct or consistent one. It may push the model to output a value even when the source is contradictory.

questions.mindset: Capture both sides of a conflict and let deterministic code flag it.

questions.scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration: the PR reviewer emits structured findings (file, line, category, severity, message). Developers can click 'dismiss' on a finding, and the dismissal rate is now 45%. The team lead wants a data-driven way to decide which prompt criteria to tighten, instead of guessing.
questions.stem: What is the MOST effective addition to the feedback loop?

options.text: Add a likely_false_positive score that the model fills in for each finding, and hide any finding whose score is above a fixed threshold before it is posted.
Run a second, fully independent reviewer instance on every pull request and post only the findings that both reviewer instances agree on.
Collect developers' free-text dismissal reasons and append all of them to the review prompt on every run so the model can learn from them.
Add a detected_pattern field naming the code construct behind each finding, log dismissals against it, and analyze dismissal rates per pattern.

questions.explanation: A **detected_pattern** field makes each finding traceable to the code construct that triggered it. Joined with dismissal events, it shows **which patterns** produce false positives, so you can rewrite or disable those criteria precisely. It turns developer behavior into measurable feedback.

whyWrong.A: A model-reported false-positive score is self-assessment, which is unreliable, and it hides findings without telling you why they were wrong.
whyWrong.B: Two reviewers can reduce noise, but at double the cost, and it gives no insight into which criteria cause dismissals. It is a bigger architecture, not a feedback loop.
whyWrong.C: An ever-growing pile of raw comments bloats the prompt and gives no structured analysis. It is unbounded and hard to evaluate.

questions.mindset: Make every finding traceable to its trigger so the false positives can be measured.

questions.stem: A team moved its extraction pipeline to strict tool use with a JSON schema. An engineer proposes deleting the application-side validator because 'the schema now guarantees correct output'. Which statement BEST describes what the schema does and does not guarantee?

options.text: The schema guarantees both structure and content, so cross-field checks like totals adding up are now redundant and can be removed from the pipeline.
The validator is only needed when the stop reason is refusal; for every other stop reason the output is already guaranteed to be valid and correct.
The schema guarantees well-formed, schema-shaped output but not semantic correctness, so business checks such as sums and field placement remain needed in code.
The schema guarantees correctness for flat top-level objects only, so validation should be kept just for nested arrays such as invoice line items.

questions.explanation: Structured outputs and strict tool use constrain output to the **schema's syntax and shape**. They do not make values **correct**: line items can still fail to sum, values can land in the wrong field, and data can be invented when the source lacks it. Application-side semantic validation stays in the loop.

whyWrong.A: Schema compliance is about structure. It does not check business rules such as sums or cross-field consistency.
whyWrong.B: Refusals and max_tokens truncation are both cases where output may not match the schema, and even normal completions are not guaranteed to be semantically correct (the docs also note enum casing is not guaranteed). A validator is needed regardless of stop reason.
whyWrong.D: Nesting has nothing to do with it. Flat and nested outputs alike are only guaranteed to be well-formed.

questions.mindset: A schema guarantees the shape of the output, not that the values are right.

questions.stem: You are designing the validation-retry loop for a high-volume document extraction service that feeds a finance system. Which TWO design choices are MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Cap the number of retry attempts per document and send documents that still fail validation to a human review queue with the errors attached.
Keep retrying each failed document until it passes validation, because every failure can eventually be fixed with enough attempts and enough feedback.
On each retry, send the source document, the previous failed output and the specific validation errors so the model can target the exact fix.
On each retry, leave out the previous failed output so the model is not anchored on its mistake, and resend only the original request text.
After two failures on a field, disable that field's validation for the document so the extraction can still reach the finance system on time.

questions.explanation: A sound loop is **bounded** and **informative**. Each retry carries the document, the failed output and the specific errors so the model can self-correct (C). A cap plus escalation (A) stops wasted spend on failures retries cannot fix, such as data missing from the source, and keeps a human in the loop for a finance system.

whyWrong.B: Unbounded retries waste cost and can never fix data that is absent from the source. Repeated pressure can produce a fabricated value that happens to pass validation.
whyWrong.D: Without the failed output and errors, the retry is effectively blind. The model has no information about what to change.
whyWrong.E: Turning off validation lets known-bad data into a finance system. A failure should go to a human, not be waved through.

questions.mindset: Retry with specific feedback, cap the attempts, then hand off to a human.

questions.scenario: Multi-Agent Research System: the report-generation subagent receives a numbered source list from the coordinator and must cite every claim as [S#]. A spot check finds that about 5% of reports cite source IDs that do not exist in the list, such as [S14] when only 11 sources were provided. These reports go to clients, so the most reliable fix is needed.

options.text: Validate every citation ID in code against the provided source list; on failure, retry with the invalid IDs and the list, and mark any still-unsupported claims.
Add a clear instruction to the report subagent's system prompt stating that it must never cite a source ID that does not appear in the provided list.
Ask the report subagent to re-read its own draft at the end of the same response and to correct any citations that look wrong to it before returning.
Add several few-shot examples of correctly cited reports to the prompt so that the model consistently imitates proper citation behavior in every run.

questions.explanation: Checking that every cited ID exists is a **deterministic** rule, so it belongs in code, not in a prompt. A validator catches 100% of invalid IDs. The retry then gets **specific feedback** (which IDs are invalid, plus the real list), and any claim that still cannot be tied to a source is marked unsupported instead of shipping with a fake citation. This is the most reliable option for client-facing output.

whyWrong.B: A prompt instruction may reduce the rate, but it guarantees nothing. When a check can be done in code, a prompt-only control is the weaker choice for client-facing reports.
whyWrong.C: Having the model verify its own citations is a recognized hallucination-reduction technique, but it stays probabilistic and shares the draft's blind spots. When the rule (ID must exist in the list) is checkable in code, the code check is the reliable control.
whyWrong.D: Examples help with format, but they do not verify IDs against this report's actual source list. Invalid citations can still get through.

questions.mindset: If a rule can be checked in code, check it in code and send the specific failure back to the model.
